title: Fish Goujons
subtitle: Panko-crumbed fish strips for the whole table
excerpt: Fish goujons are white fish fillets cut into thin strips, coated in seasoned breadcrumbs, and fried until crisp and golden. Faster than a whole battered fish and easier to eat by younger children. Serve with tartare sauce, ketchup, or a squeeze of lemon.
sourceNotes: Fish goujons are a standard of British home cooking and pub menus, drawing on the French goujon (thin strip of fish) served since at least the 1970s in UK restaurants. The panko coating is a modern adaptation of the classic seasoned flour-and-egg method.

recipe.freezeNotes: Coat the fish and freeze raw on a tray, then transfer to a freezer bag. Cook from frozen at 200°C for 18 to 20 minutes.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Coat the goujons up to 2 hours ahead and keep on a tray in the fridge uncovered. Fry just before serving.

content.text: Fish goujons are strips of white fish coated in crisp breadcrumbs and shallow-fried in minutes. They give you all the pleasure of battered fish in a lighter, quicker form that is easier to cook at home than a deep-fry. Cod, haddock, or pollock all work; the key is to cut the strips evenly so they cook at the same rate.
Cut and set up the coating station
Pat {{cod-fillet}} cod fillets dry with kitchen paper. Cut each fillet diagonally into strips about 2 cm wide. Drying the fish helps the flour stick and reduces spitting in the pan.

Set out three shallow dishes: one with {{plain-flour}} of seasoned flour, one with {{eggs}} beaten eggs, and one with {{breadcrumbs-panko}} of panko breadcrumbs. Season the flour with the sea salt and pepper.

Working one strip at a time, dust the fish in the flour and shake off any excess. Dip in the beaten egg to coat fully, then press into the panko so the strip is covered on all sides. Set on a plate and repeat with the remaining strips.

Heat {{sunflower-oil}} of sunflower oil in a large frying pan over a medium-high heat. When the oil shimmers and a breadcrumb dropped in sizzles immediately, add the goujons in a single layer. Do not crowd the pan; cook in two batches if needed.

Cook for 3 to 4 minutes on one side without moving until golden brown underneath. Turn with tongs and cook for another 2 to 3 minutes until golden all over and the fish is cooked through. Lift onto a plate lined with kitchen paper to drain briefly, then serve immediately with lemon wedges.

items.symptom: The coating is falling off in the pan
items.cause: The flour was not shaken off before dipping in egg, so the egg layer is patchy. Or the oil was not hot enough when the fish went in.
items.fix: Make sure each strip is lightly dusted with flour first, then fully coated in egg, then pressed firmly into the panko. Test the oil with one breadcrumb before adding the fish.

items.symptom: The breadcrumbs are browning but the fish is still raw inside
items.cause: The oil temperature is too high, or the strips are too thick.
items.fix: Reduce the heat slightly and turn the goujons earlier. Cut the fish strips no thicker than 2 cm. A strip of cod 2 cm thick cooks through in 6 to 7 minutes total over medium-high heat.

items.symptom: The fish strips are soggy, not crisp
items.cause: The fish was not dried before coating, the oil was too cool, or the pan was overcrowded.
items.fix: Always pat the fish dry before coating. Cook in batches and keep the heat high enough that the oil sizzles steadily around the goujons.

items.symptom: The goujons stick to the pan
items.cause: Not enough oil, or the pan was moved too soon before the coating had set.
items.fix: Use a generous amount of oil and let the goujons sit undisturbed for at least 3 minutes before checking. They will release naturally once the coating is golden.

content.text: Goujons began as a French restaurant preparation, the word taken from the small freshwater gudgeon fish that were once served this way. British pub menus adopted the style in the 1970s and early 1980s, applying it to cod and plaice cut into uniform strips for fast frying. At home they are a reliable weeknight supper and a good way to introduce children to fish: no bones, no skin, familiar crunch. Tartare sauce is the classic pairing; ketchup is perfectly acceptable.
